{{Short description|Mathematics education system}}
[[Image:Kent_Mathematics_Project,_Test_Book,_Level_1.jpg|right|thumb|Front cover of K.M.P. Test Book level 1.]]
The '''Kent Mathematics Project''' (K.M.P.) was an educational system for teaching mathematics to 9-16 year olds. The system comprised task worksheets, booklets, audio [[compact cassette]]s and tests. Through the 1970s and 1980s, it was widely adopted in [[Kent]] schools, as well as being exported internationally.<ref name="Banks1985">{{cite journal|title=Ed Tech from Programs to Material‐Bank in the KMP|year=1985 |doi=10.1080/1355800850220109|last1=Banks |first1=Bertram |journal=Plet: Programmed Learning & Educational Technology |volume=22 |pages=57–62 }}</ref>

The system was based on the idea that:

{{quote|mathematical learning should be in terms of levels of concept development and that chronological age should not be the basis of course design.<ref>{{cite book|first1=Leslie|last1=Beckett|title=Maintaining Choice in the Secondary Curriculum: Report of an Investigation Into the Problems Caused by Falling Rolls|publisher=Council for Educational Technology|date=1981}}</ref>}}

K.M.P. providing materials and structure for non-specialist teachers to teach math classes while sharing the effort required in producing suitable teaching material.

==History==

Started in 1966, the project originated at Ridgewaye School, [[Southborough, Kent|Southborough]], [[Tunbridge Wells]] which closed its doors in 1991. K.M.P went through several titles including "An Auto-Instructional Course in Mathematics" and "The Ridgewaye Individualized Course". The system was inspired by the self-directed learning of the [[Dalton Plan]] while attempting to avoid its pitfalls.<ref name="Banks1971">{{cite journal|first1=Bertram|last1=Banks|title=The "Disaster Kit"|journal=The Mathematical Gazette|volume=55|issue=391|date=Feb 1971|pages=17–22|doi=10.2307/3613300|jstor=3613300 |s2cid=185021528 }}</ref> K.M.P was gradually extended over time, involving trials at a number of schools before being more widely distributed.<ref name="Banks1975">{{cite journal|first1=Bertram|last1=Banks|title=The Kent Mathematics Project and Educational Technology|journal=Mathematics in School|volume=4|issue=3|date=May 1975|pages=2–4}}</ref> K.M.P. was adopted by the education authority in 1970<ref name="Little">{{cite journal|title=Types of Assessment and Interest in Learning: variation in the South of England in the 1980s|year=1994 |doi=10.1080/0969594940010205|last1=Little |first1=Angela |journal=Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy & Practice |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=201–222 }}</ref> and used in over seventy schools around Kent.<ref name="Neal"/>

In 1988, the project's director objected to the [[National Curriculum (England, Wales and Northern Ireland)|National Curriculum]] which emphasised goals to be achieved by particular ages.<ref name="Larcomb">{{cite journal|first1=Tony|last1=Larcomb|title=Mathematics: Prospects and Problems|journal=British Journal of Special Education|volume=15|issue=4|date=1988}}</ref>

==Usage==

To teach a specific concept, the teacher selected a set of twelve tasks called a "matrix" from a material bank for the pupil to complete. The teacher was expected to be available to mentor pupils if they encountered difficulty. The tasks were completed in any order, then self-corrected by the pupil and checked by the teacher. When the entire task matrix is completed, the pupil performed a test to check their understanding. The tests results were then used by the teacher to construct the next task matrix.<ref name="Little"/> This allowed children to progress at their own rate, either ahead<ref name="Maltby">{{cite journal|doi=10.1177/026142948600400207|title=Educational Provision for Gifted Children|year=1986 |last1=Maltby |first1=Florence |journal=Gifted Education International |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=97–100 |s2cid=145439228 }}</ref> or behind the rest of the class, while allowing the teacher to customize the course to the pupil's needs. Tasks were assigned a level of 1 to 9, depending on their difficulty. The difficulty of tasks assigned was based on the child's ability, rather than their age.<ref name="Wiliam">{{cite book|last1=Wiliam|first1=D.|date=2007|chapter=Once you know what they’ve learned, what do you do next? Designing curriculum and assessment for growth|editor-first1=R.|editor-last1=Lissitz|title=Assessing and modeling cognitive development in schools|publisher=Maple Grove, MN: JAM Press.}}</ref>

KMP materials were published by [[Ward Lock & Co]].

==Impact==

Ideas from K.M.P. were adopted in later teaching tools, including Graded Assessment in Mathematics (GAIM) and Secondary Mathematics Individualised Learning Experiment (SMILE).<ref name="Neal">{{cite book|first1=D.M.|last1=Neal|title=Teaching Maths|publisher=Taylor & Francis Ltd|date=1982-09-09}}</ref>
